content: The elementary charge, denoted as ( e ), is the electric charge carried by a single proton. Equivalently, it is the negative of the electric charge carried by a single electron. This charge is a fundamental physical constant and serves as the unit of electric charge in the system of atomic units and other natural unit systems.602176487 times 10^{-19} , text{C} ). The uncertainty in this value is detailed in the CODATA report, specifically in Table XLVIII. In the centimetre-gram-second (CGS) system of units, the elementary charge is expressed as ( 4.803204273 times 10^{-10} , text{statcoulombs} ). Since then, it has been regarded as indivisible. However, in the 1960s, the discovery of quarks introduced the concept of fractional electric charges. Quarks possess charges that are fractions of the elementary charge, specifically ( frac{1}{3}e ) and ( frac{2}{3}e ). Despite this, the term elementary charge remains practically relevant because quarks are not observed in isolation; they only exist in groupings that result in charges that are integer multiples of ( e ). In 1982, Robert Laughlin proposed the existence of fractionally charged quasiparticles to explain the fractional quantum Hall effect. Subsequently, in 1997, two independent research groups—one at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, and the other at the Commissariat à l'énergie atomique laboratory near Paris—reported the detection of such quasiparticles carrying an electric current.
